title: Tense Presidential Elections, a Focus on Domestic Audiences and Oscars Closer Than Ever: 10 Takeaways From the Rio Film Festival
description: Hosting a film festival during historic presidential elections destined to shape an entire country’s future is a hefty ask, but this year’s Rio Film
body:
Hosting a film festival during historic presidential elections destined to shape an entire country’s future is a hefty ask, but this year’s Rio Film Festival managed to carefully and purposefully thread the lines between focusing on the cinema and the industry of today and not turning a blind eye to the issues of tomorrow.

	This year’s edition, which ran Oct. 1-11, was bookended by two buzzy queer films in Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s “La Bola Negra” and Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid,” and introduced audiences to a promising crop of Brazilian cinema. Major national titles at the festival included Gabriel Martins’s Toronto-selected “On Behalf of My Son,” Allan Deberton’s Oscar hopeful “Gugu’s World,” Enock Carvalho and Mateus Farias’s Locarno-winning “The Riverbank,” and Venice Queer Lion winner “London,” by Victor di Marco and Márcio Picoli.
	

	The bright corridors of RioMarket were also filled with enthusiastic industry experts and producers queuing up for sessions on burning issues like Artificial Intelligence and audience development through TikTok. Below, Variety’s main takeaways from this year’s festival, from the strong presence of young audiences to narrower bridges to Spain and a market focus on domestic audiences.


	Politics at the centre

	There was no escape. With the festival’s first weekend coinciding with the Brazilian presidential elections, almost every conversation overheard at RioMarket during the event’s early days was intertwined with politics. Following the result of the first round, which saw current president Luis Inácio Lula da Silva lose to far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro by less than 2%, Variety published an in-depth report on the consequences of a possible Bolsonaro mandate for the country’s burgeoning cinema. Two days later, Variety also broke the news of how several high-profile Brazilian film figures — including Kleber Mendonça Filho, Wagner Moura, Fernando Meirelles and Petra Costa — signed an open letter calling international attention to the upcoming second round of elections, taking place on Oct. 25.
	

	Despite the tensions brought up by the elections, there was a latent sense of camaraderie and hope at the festival in the days since the first round at the polls. Several filmmakers have taken up to the stage at the festival to declare their support of Lula, including “Club Kid” director Jordan Firstman, who raised his hand into an “L” sign while introducing the festival’s closing film at the Odeon on Saturday night.



	

					Jordan Firstman makes an ‘L’ sign with his hand at the Rio Film Festival, courtesy of David Campana
	



	Audience development needs screening rooms

	At several of this year’s panels at the festival’s industry sidebar, RioMarket, key executives and producers frequently mentioned the need for audience development in Brazil. The consensus was that the country offers already eager cinephiles, with many young audiences well-versed in international cinema thanks to healthy online communities, but there is still a challenge when it comes to converting those film fans into cinema-goers. In one of the festival’s first industry sessions, an in-conversation event with director Marcelo Gomes and Rodrigo Santoro, festival director Ilda Santiago brought up a burning issue: the still small number of cinema theater screens in Brazil.

	The country currently has 3.538 screens, with 43% of these concentrated in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The number is still very low when considering Brazil has a population of over 214 million. For reference, the U.S. boasts 35,000 to 40,000 commercial screens for a population of 349 million, and France has 6,355 screens for a population of 69 million.

	A co-production power

	Following two banner years of international success with Walter Salles’s “I’m Still Here” and Kleber Mendonça Filho’s “The Secret Agent,” this year saw Brazil make a splash at international festivals with high-profile co-productions. Examples include Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog,” Marcelo Martinessi’s “Narciso,” Benjamin Naishtat’s “Glaxo,” Marco Becchis’ “Back to Buenos Aires,” Dominga Sotomayor’s “La Perra,” and Bruno Santamaría Razo’s “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building.”

	This momentum confirmed itself at the festival. Leading production banners such as MyMama Entertainment and Bubbles Project announced upcoming projects during the event, with the former working on Locarno-winner Andrea Štaka’s “Ibicaba: O Paraíso Prometido,” starring Ella Rumpf and Júlio Andrade, and the latter gearing up to shoot “Puan” helmer Maria Alché’s “I Love You, and Today Everything Looks Beautiful.” Several producers have also spoken at industry panels on the importance of finding global partners and alternative financing structures, especially at times of political instability that could see Brazil’s public funds shrink or collapse in the near future.
	



	

					Courtesy of Xande Sequeiros
									Xande Sequeiros
	



	Domestic audiences matter

	While international co-productions are on the up and up, Brazilian producers have reiterated the importance of making films for their domestic audiences. Brazil is a massive market, with keen, enthusiastic audiences that still largely consume foreign films and television, but savvy producers and filmmakers are working to change this trend. Gustavo Mello, partner at major Boutique Filmes banner, told Variety that, since their highly successful Netflix series “3%,” Brazil has remained their top priority. “We need to produce for Brazil, and it needs to remain our focus. When we do this well, our work travels.”

	Festival director Ilda Santiago is echoing this movement in her programming of Premiere Brasil, the festival’s section dedicated to Brazilian cinema, which has expanded into several subcategories in recent years. “Brazilian cinema isn’t one singular thing,” she tells Variety. “Our cinema is plural. I don’t want audiences to say they are going to the cinema to watch a Brazilian film; I want them to seek genre films, dramas, coming-of-agers, which just so happen to be Brazilian.”

	The kids are alright

	In a year where the success of Kane Parsons’s “Backrooms” and Curry Barker’s “Obsession” sent the industry into a frenzy, there’s a latent sense of hope for young audiences returning to cinemas. This was proven true in Rio, where young cinephiles lined up outside festival venues, enthusiastically discussing upcoming screenings while scrolling their Letterboxd accounts. Interestingly, young audiences could be seen not only at screenings of major international hits, but also lining up for more obscure festival titles and filling up industry sessions at RioMarket, too. It was heartening to watch attentive school students sit through a key industry session on women in cinema delivered in partnership with the European Film Promotion, and to hear the hubbub of excitable cinephiles gearing up to enter a free screening of “Gugu’s World” at the beautiful FGV Cultural Centre venue.

	Genre is key…

	Founder of Mórbido Film Fest and executive director of the Fantastic Pavilion at the Marché du Film, Pablo Guisa Koestinger was in Rio for the first time to launch Fantastic: Brasil at the festival. The new industry platform for genre cinema in the country is a partnership between the Fantastic Pavilion Cannes, Rio Market, Festival do Rio, FICCI Industria, #LINK Documentary Industry Meeting, Mórbido Film Fest, and Sitges, and launched three calls for emerging voices in Latin American genre cinema.
	

	Highlights of Brazilian cinema at this year’s festival were also genre titles, including Maju de Paiva and Bernardo Florim’s “Diário do Fogo,” Ricardo Alves Jr.’s psychological thriller “The French Teacher,” and Gustavo Vinagre and Gurcius Gewdner’s B-movie extravaganza “Bowels of Hell.”

	… But not just horror

	While horror remains king in terms of genre films attracting audiences at the festival, this year’s program showcased how Brazilian filmmakers are taking interesting risks within other genres. Tomás Portella’s “Overman” is the Brazilian response to the Marvel Cinematic Universe — adapted from the comic strips by famed cartoonist Laerte, the film sees star Caco Ciocler play the titular sex-addict superhero in a delightful romp that includes bad guys that torment citizens with stinky farts and an arch-enemy called Dirty Capitalist.

	Speaking of delightful, “My First Girlfriend” is another major festival standout. The romantic comedy reunites “City of God” director Kátia Lund with the film’s star Jonathan Haagensen, with the duo co-directing a charming, deeply Brazilian love story led by a promising young cast that includes Faíska Alves, Cecilia Sanchez, Pedro Ottoni and Jordana Morena. Lastly, “Rio” and “Ice Age” director Carlos Saldanha brought Brazil into the realm of the blockbuster adventure film with the ambitious Brazilian closing gala “100 Days,” chronicling Amyr Klink’s pioneering crossing of the Atlantic Ocean in a small rowing boat.



	

					100 Days
									Courtesy of Fábio Braga, Pivô Audiovisual
	



	A sturdy bridge to Spain

	It was only fitting that Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s Cannes sensation “La Bola Negra” opened this year’s festival given the heavy Spanish presence on the ground in Rio. Veteran Spanish producer Esther García, a longtime collaborator of Pedro Almodóvar’s, presided over this year’s Premiere Brasil jury, while several standout Spanish films played in the program. Titles include Diego Luna’s “Ashes,” Júlia de Paz Solvas’s “The Good Daughter,” and Ian De La Rosa’s “Iván & Hadoum.”

	Santiago tells Variety the relationship between Spain and Brazil is a “natural” one, and a bridge that feels ever-strengthened by Brazilians’s growing identification with their Latin roots and interest in Spanish-speaking stories. “Today, I see young people in Brazil actively trying to learn Spanish, which is something I didn’t see 10 years ago,” she says. “There’s this latent desire from a new Brazilian generation to be connected with their Latin heritage and cultural identity.”
	

	“Brazilian cinema wants to be in conversation with Latin cinema, and Latin cinema wants to tap into the huge market that is Brazil,” she adds. “Spain consolidates a lot of Spanish-speaking cinema, and I believe it is the ideal partner to allow us to grow as an industry and build more and more partnerships with the world.”

	Real life is a real draw

	Turning a corner at Rio’s buzzing Botafogo neighborhood, one would expect the lengthy queues to be for a screening of major festival hits such as “Wild Horse Nine” or “Coward,” but while those films still attracted hordes, some of the longest queues at this year’s festival were for films telling the real-life stories of Brazilian legends. Pedro Waddington’s “Fernanda,” which turns on the career of legendary “Central Station” actress Fernanda Montenegro, was one of the most popular films on the ground, with other buzzy titles including Prime Video’s “Marília Mendonça – Um Sentimento Louco,” Eryk Rocha’s “Elza” and Renato Terra, Marcos Caetano, and Leo Caetano’s “Alucinação.”

	Oscars closer than ever

	Over the last two years, thanks to “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent,” the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has realized the unparalleled passion of Brazilians online. Last year, Academy CEO Bill Kramer attended the Rio Film Festival for the first time, where he said the furore over Salles’s film was “historic.” “It was exciting to see the growth in our social media channels and the increased audience in Latin America,” he added. “It was incredible to watch videos of people stopping their Carnival celebrations to watch the awards.”

	This year, the festival reiterated its partnership with the Academy by inviting Michael Benedict, director of member relations and awards administration, and Taylor Morales, associate director of the film archive – film preservation and public access, to speak at RioMarket. The Academy representatives spoke about Brazil’s importance to the organization, with Benedict noting their “increased” focus on “global cinema” after telling keen audiences how to submit their films to the Oscars.

schema.headline: Tense Presidential Elections, a Focus on Domestic Audiences and Oscars Closer Than Ever: 10 Takeaways From the Rio Film Festival

title: ‘Silver Express’ Review: Miki Tanaka’s Sensitive Debut Feature Explores Asexual and Aromantic Identity
description: There are films and series with asexual characters in them, but far fewer interested in the experiential questions about moving through society as a
body:
There are films and series with asexual characters in them, but far fewer interested in the experiential questions about moving through society as asexual and aromantic, and considering that identity on a spectrum. Miki Tanaka‘s debut feature “Silver Express” is one such film: a gentle character study observing the everyday annoyances of an asexual person living amongst people who not only don’t understand her, but insist on her adaptation to a heteronormative lifestyle. “Silver Express” wonders what common language can be found to relay the breadth of that orientation to others — and get those people to relax about setting them up.
	

	A lot of the time, the protagonist Chieri (newcomer Yui Okamoto, in a performance that delicately embodies the character’s uncertainty) is faced with people — no matter how well-meaning — presenting the idea to her that the right relationship will change her aromanticism and asexuality, that there’s just an experience she has missed. Chieri sometimes tunes out of these conversations, keenly listening for a sound that others can’t seem to hear: a train. 


	Later, she explains that she thinks of the train (the “Silver Express” of the title) as something traveling to a final stop where special “silver lions” reside — her euphemistic term for herself and perhaps other aromantics and asexuals. (“They don’t fit into a pride of ordinary lions,” she says). Euphemism is important in “Silver Express”: Chieri and others often talk around her orientation because there’s a linguistic gap; “asexuality” is itself a term which doesn’t exist in an exact sense in Japanese, having only made its way into common parlance as a loan word in the past 10 to 15 years. (There is a longer and more complex linguistic discussion to be had, by those more qualified, on evolving LGBTQ+ terminology in the country and how this matches up against older concepts.)
	

	While it does consider a sort of struggling common language (or at least, a definitive shorthand) around asexuality, “Silver Express” is for the most part interested in how that hazy definition, or continuing adjustment to a definition, is experienced on a personal level, as the loneliness of moving against the current. Tanaka’s film doesn’t assume that platonic relationships between men and women are a pipe dream — it just so happens that Chieri keeps running into people with “ulterior motives.”

	That is, until she meets fellow aromantic (but crucially, not asexual) Shoya, played by Hayato Kurihara. The two hit it off, he doesn’t balk at or laugh at her admission that she doesn’t understand romantic attraction, and casually mentions that he doesn’t get it either. And the film seems warmer again — finally, a relationship with no ulterior motive (perhaps). Either way, they’re close, sometimes even sleeping in each other’s arms. It’s part of the myriad ways the film is interested in different degrees of intimacy and love, such as with Chieri’s friend and one time roommate Yuki — a character who in part acts as a helpful marker of time via her career, marriage and pregnancy, while Chieri mostly seems content carrying on doing what she likes.

	The film moves at a casual clip, as conversations and relationships flow quickly across days and locations. The elliptical passage of time across the film’s broader structure also manifests more directly in how Tanaka shapes a scene, sometimes cutting off before the final word spoken.

	It’s part of how the film gently embodies, or at least falls in tune with, Chieri’s subjective worldview. To her, romance and courtship isn’t just ambient but invasive, robbing her of friends — both in the sense that men can’t seem to leave things platonic, while women either mock her or shun her in favor of a new date. Tanaka emphasizes this by taking any stylistic romanticism out of the score, which embraces discordance, and cinematography: when Chieri’s friends make her feel unwelcome, harsh, cold lighting underlines that sense. This makes Chieri’s moments of intimacy stand out all the more, as warmth returns in scenes with long-time friend Yuki and new friend Shoya.

	That said, part of what makes Tanaka’s exploration work is recognizing that Chieri’s struggle to fit in isn’t entirely predicated on her asexuality and aromanticism: There’s some good old-fashioned social awkwardness at play too. She sometimes acts with outright hostility at the drop of a hat, though there is often good reason for this frustration. For all the subtleties of Okamoto’s performance and the film’s framing thereof, it occasionally resorts to clichés to communicate her closed-off nature — as when a teacher starts lecturing about the very thing on her mind. 
	

	But these are minor missteps, considering the language gap around asexuality and aromanticism in Japan. It feels less egregious when a scene features a group of friends sitting around a table, literally attempting to map out the respective sexual orientations of Chieri and Shoyo, trying to understand where they overlap and where they don’t. It’s a credit to the light touch of “Silver Express” that any potential instructiveness rarely feels that way.

schema.headline: ‘Silver Express’ Review: Miki Tanaka’s Sensitive Debut Feature Explores Asexual and Aromantic Identity

title: Piracy in the Crosshairs: Brazil to Launch Campaign Against IP Theft
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Brazil’s Audiovisual Industry and Commerce Federation (FICA) announced at the Rio Film Festival’s RioMarket the launch at t
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Brazil’s Audiovisual Industry and Commerce Federation (FICA) announced at the Rio Film Festival’s RioMarket the launch at the end of October of an anti-piracy awareness campaign in free-to-air and pay television, radio, out-of-home (OOH) advertising and movie theaters.

	Local media, telecom and exhibition groups are supporting the campaign by providing free advertising space on their platforms. Local ad agency 11:21 created the pro bono advertising campaign, which will initially reach São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro, the three most populous states in Brazil, and eventually be expanded countrywide, 11:21’s CEO Gustavo Bastos told Variety.
	

	“The theft of intellectual property is a problem that must be tackled worldwide. The loss of revenue is enormous and affects the entire audiovisual industry ecosystem. What is even more concerning is that ordinary people do not realize the implications of their actions when they use, for example, an illegal TV box,” Walkiria Barbosa, president of FICA, told Variety. “Fortunately, we have managed to bring together major partners to launch this far-reaching campaign, which is now getting underway.”


	Disque Denúncia, a Brazilian anonymous crime-reporting hotline, is a campaign partner. The initiative allows citizens to report suspected criminal activities without revealing their identities.

	Bastos said the campaign will use the language of films and series to communicate the danger of piracy. They created pirate characters for the campaign inspired by pirate productions.
	

	“Anti-piracy campaigns generally adopt a law-enforcement tone, emphasizing repression, which tends to alienate audiences. We chose a cinematic approach instead, drawing inspiration from pirate productions,” Bastos said.



	

					Gustavo Bastos
									Credit: Felipe Mariano
	



	A 2022 study of Brazil’s Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) pointed out that piracy caused annual losses of 12 billion reais ($2.4 billion) in the country, Jonas Antunes Couto, president of the Brazilian Pay-TV Association (ABTA), told Variety. The study also identified piracy practices in about 4.5 million households in Brazil.

	According to Couto, illegal TV boxes, mostly smuggled from Asia, have become the major concern in Brazil’s fight against audiovisual piracy. These devices allow consumers to access movies, television series, live sports broadcasts and other content without authorization from copyright holders. Connected to TV sets and the internet, these relatively inexpensive devices can provide access to vast libraries of pirated content, often eliminating the need for legitimate streaming subscriptions or pay-TV services.

	“Piracy is a global phenomenon. In our view, those behind this business are not small-scale operators, but large criminal organizations that engage in other illegal activities, including cybercrime, to finance their operations,” Couto said.

	Beyond the financial damage inflicted on pay-TV operators, streaming platforms and audiovisual producers, distributors and exhibitors, illegal TV boxes may also pose significant cybersecurity risks, as they may contain malware that can expose users to data theft, unauthorized access to personal information and other cyber threats.

	Claro is one of the corporations supporting the campaign. In addition to mobile and fixed-line telephony and high-speed broadband internet, Claro offers in Brazil pay-TV and digital entertainment services and is directly affected by piracy.

	“A major anti-piracy operation carried out in Argentina last year succeeded in shutting down one of Latin America’s largest hubs for pirated content. In the three months following the operation, sales of pay-TV subscription packages in Brazil increased by more than 20%,” said Fernando Magalhães, Claro’s director of programing and content. “But it’s a cat-and-mouse game. As anti-piracy efforts become more technologically sophisticated, piracy itself evolves technologically as well.”



	

									Courtesy of 11:21

schema.headline: Piracy in the Crosshairs: Brazil to Launch Campaign Against IP Theft

title: Pasto Cine Boards ‘Puan’ Helmer María Alché’s ‘I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Argentina’s Pasto Cine has boarded María Alché’s upcoming “I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful.” The film is pr
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil – Argentina’s Pasto Cine has boarded María Alché’s upcoming “I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful.” The film is produced by leading Brazilian banner Bubbles Project alongside Spain’s Elastica Films, Germany’s Pandora Film, and France’s Maneki Films.

	“I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful” is set between the 1950s and 1960s and trails the lives of Josefina and Jorge following the death of their parents. Orphaned, the children are taken in by their irreverent aunt Berta, and begin a new life in the big city in a house frequented by intellectuals and where all kinds of political conspiracies are hatched. In her director’s statement, Alché said the film is “based on the creation of a group of strong, complex and magnetic characters who survive thanks to a mystical and everyday quality: faith in life and the ability to laugh at tragedy.”
	

	“In her personal orphanhood, Josefina recognizes an unlikely empathy with the dispossessed in Argentina, historical orphans adopted by the maternal Eva Perón,” added the director. “In today’s Argentina, overshadowed by the rise of the extreme right that shamelessly evokes the days of military rule, I am interested in recovering that past when the country still had a productive matrix and there was hope for the future.”


	Actress, screenwriter, and director Alché wrote and directed “Puan” alongside Benjamín Naishtat (“Glaxo”). The film won the Silver Shell for Actor and Screenplay at the San Sebastián Film Festival, was nominated for the Goya Awards, and was a box office hit in Argentina. 
	

	She co-wrote Lucrecia Martel’s “Nuestra tierra” and wrote and directed the feature film “A Family Submerged,” which won the Horizontes Latinos Award in San Sebastián, the Ingmar Bergman Award for Best First Feature at the Goteborg Film Festival, Best Screenplay at the Lima Film Festival, and Best Director at Ficunam.



	

					‘Puan,’ courtesy of Luxbox
	



	Alché’s latest is currently in the financing stages and is aiming to shoot in the second half of 2027. Renowned French cinematographer Hélène Louvart (“La Chimera,” “The Lost Daughter”) has also joined the project, as have “Divine Love” editor Livia Serpa and “I’m Still Here” sound director Laura Zimerman. This is the third collaboration between the Argentinian director and Tatiana Leite’s Bubbles Project, and the fourth collaboration between Bubbles and Barbara Francisco’s Pasto Cine.

	“My collaboration with Bárbara Francisco of Pasto Cine, whom I met during the EAVE Puentes workshop in 2013, and with director María Alché, goes back more than a decade,” Leite tells Variety. “María makes singular films, and I am fascinated by her direction of actors and by the dreamlike dimension that permeates reality in her work.”

	“When they sent me the screenplay for ‘I Love You and Today Everything Looks Beautiful,’ I discovered something even more precious in my reading, something that moved me deeply from beginning to end,” she adds. “‘I Love You’ is a period film, yet it feels entirely relevant to the world we live in today.”

	Francisco notes how a large part of the film’s team, including Louvart and Serpa, “has shared a close and lasting bond since working together on ‘A Family Submerged.’” “This bond is rooted in a shared vision of the world and a common approach to filmmaking. For María Alché’s new film, I’m once again delighted to join forces with Tatiana Leite, Christoph Friedel (Pandora), and welcome Elastica Films in Spain and Maneki Films in France”.

	Bubbles Project is one of Brazil’s leading co-production forces, having recently been involved in high-profile projects such as Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” and Pedro Pinho’s “I Only Rest in the Storm.” They have recently wrapped shooting on Miguel Gomes’s “Selvajaria,” which was filmed in Bahia, and are in development on “May God Repay You” by “Benzinho” director Gustavo Pizzi, “Dora and Vera” by “Malu” director Pedro Freire, and Valentina Homem’s feature debut “Under de Baobab Tree.”

title: Cannes Festival Winning Producer Quijote Films Launches In-House Scripted Series Division (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Chile’s Quijote Films, behind Cannes Un Certain Regard prizewinners “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo” and “The Settlers,” is venturing into scri
body:
Chile’s Quijote Films, behind Cannes Un Certain Regard prizewinners “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo” and “The Settlers,” is venturing into scripted series with the launch of a new in-house series development arm.

	Based out of Chile and Los Angeles, the company has already invested up to $250,000 in development ahead of Mipcom, which Quijote head of strategy Sergio Karmy is attending.


	Known for its savvy assembling of multiple territories to co-produce auteur projects, Quijote Films has lead produced or participated in close to 30 international co-productions to date, including Chile’s first co-production pacts with Ukraine (“Pamfir”) and South Africa (“The Smell of Apples”).
	

	“We’ve shown that independent, auteur-driven cinema can be a viable business. I’m proud that at Quijote we’ve reversed the usual formula: our arthouse films are allowing us to finance our expansion into new genres, formats and more commercial audiences,” said Quijote CEO Giancarlo Nasi.

	The company’s roughly $250,000 investment in 2026 supports creative personnel and project-specific costs aimed at building a sustainable pipeline of original series. It has established an in-house screenwriting and external development team to originate original series and partner with third-party creators, studios and production companies as an executive producer.

	Buttressing its co-production efforts in Chile is the country’s cash rebate incentive that reimburses between 30% and 40% of expenses incurred by international productions filmed in Chile.
	

	It applies to feature films and series with a minimum investment of $400,000, allowing productions to recover between $120,000 and $3 million.

	“Our mission is clear: to create high-quality content in partnership with key players across different regions, while preserving the identity and reputation that independent cinema has helped Quijote build over the years. We’re incredibly excited about where we stand today, how far Quijote has come, and the opportunities that lie ahead,” said Karmy, who joined Quijote from Fabula, run by director Pablo Larrain (“My Sad Dead,” “The Count”) and his producing partner Juan de Dios Larrain.

	At Mipcom, Quijote is seeking international co-development and co-financing partnerships with streaming platforms, studios and production companies. Combining original IP development with executive production and international co-production expertise, the company aims to expand its global footprint and build a pipeline of premium scripted series for worldwide audiences.

	Looking ahead to 2027, Quijote welcomes co-development opportunities across territories and languages, with no geographical or linguistic boundaries.

	“We, independent producers, have a lot to bring to the table: we have a meticulous eye for detail, know how to produce efficiently, put together co-financing structures, and work with teams across countries and cultures,” said Nasi, who in his recent Masterclass at the Vancouver Film Festival, stressed that the best-co-productions are those that make both creative and financial sense.

	“We’re still Quijote. We’re looking to replicate our co-production experience by looking for international partners who can help us bring out the best in every story, with the same exacting creative and production standards that define our work, whatever the genre or format.”

schema.headline: Cannes Festival Winning Producer Quijote Films Launches In-House Scripted Series Division (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Dan Levy Calls Out Shane Gillis’ ‘SNL’ Monologue and Says ‘More Men Need to Be Standing Up’: ‘Speechless That Something Like That Can Exist on Live National Television’
description: “Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy is calling out Shane Gillis‘ “Saturday Night Live” monologue, saying that “more men need to be standing up in opposit
body:
“Schitt’s Creek” star Dan Levy is calling out Shane Gillis‘ “Saturday Night Live” monologue, saying that “more men need to be standing up in opposition to it.” 

	Gillis, who hosted “SNL” over the weekend, has generated heated backlash for his comments about women in his opener. “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” he said. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.”
	

	Levy posted an Instagram Reel on Sunday night reacting to Gillis’ monologue in disbelief. “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists,” Levy began. “There’s a difference there. By the way, I’ve seen more men’s nipples at the gym than I’ve ever seen women showing their bodies off.”


	Levy continued,  “But I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television. And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime.'”

	The Emmy-winning actor and writer, who hosted “SNL” himself in 2021, emphasized that “men need to be defending women more.” 

	“This is not a women’s issue, this is an everybody issue. Because the more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects,” he concluded. “They are not objects. They are superior human beings to men, OK? And I’m sorry if this gets me in trouble with the internet, but fuck.” 
	

	Levy received plenty of celebrity support in the comments, with Elizabeth Banks writing “Nailed it” and Broadway actor Barrett Wilbert Weed commenting “I love you, Dan.” 

	Gillis also dropped the f-bomb during his hosting stint on Saturday, a big faux pas for live television. That and his monologue mark the latest development in the comedian’s complicated history with “SNL.” Back in 2019, he was hired as a featured player and fired days later when podcast clips resurfaced in which he made racist and homophobic comments. He later returned as a host in February 2024 and helmed the show a second time in March 2025, making Saturday’s episode his third time hosting. 

	Representatives for “Saturday Night Live” and Gillis did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

title: Ella Rumpf, Júlio Andrade, Ana Flávia Cavalcanti to Star in Locarno Winner Andrea Staka’s ‘Ibicaba: O Paraíso Prometido’ for MyMama Entertainment (EXCLUSIVE)
description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — Ella Rumpf (“Raw,” “Couture”), Júlio Andrade (“Under Pressure”) and Ana Flávia Cavalcanti (“Baby”) are set to star in Andre
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — Ella Rumpf (“Raw,” “Couture”), Júlio Andrade (“Under Pressure”) and Ana Flávia Cavalcanti (“Baby”) are set to star in Andrea Štaka’s “Ibicaba: O Paraíso Prometido.” 

	The new film by the Golden Leopard-winning director will be produced under Brazil’s MyMama Entertainment banner in co-production with Switzerland’s Cinédokké Sagl and Brazil’s MMM Carioca.


	“Ibicaba: O Paraíso Prometido” (“Ibicaba: Promised Paradise” in literal translation) is adapted from Eveline Hasler’s novel “Ibicaba: O Paraíso nas Cabeças” and based on real-life events that took place in the titular farm in rural São Paulo. The film will be shot next year in Switzerland and Cordeirópolis, a municipality in the central region of the state of São Paulo.
	

	Set in 1855, the historical drama follows a Swiss working-class single mother who travels to Brazil, drawn by the promise of a better life but who is confronted instead with a system of debt, surveillance and exploitation within a society deeply structured by slavery. Her path crosses with that of Inocência, an enslaved Black woman who possesses healing knowledge, knows the land, and devises her own strategies of resistance.

	The historical research aiding the film is conducted in collaboration with Caróu Oliveira, a Black historian dedicated to the study of slavery and the daily lives of Black women in the 19th century. Štaka’s connection with the story dates back to her adolescence, when she discovered Hasler’s novel. The director has been learning Portuguese in preparation for the film, seeking direct communication with the cast and crew and greater proximity to the characters’ dialogues and experiences.
	

	Štaka won the Golden Leopard at Locarno and the best film award at the Sarajevo Film Festival in 2006 for “Das Fräulein.” Her following films have played at Locarno and Berlin. “Ibicaba” secured the co-production development award at the Berlinale Co-Production Market last year.

	Speaking with Variety at the Rio Film Festival, MyMama Entertainment co-founder and CEO Mayra Faour Auad says she considers her label to be “an international production company.”

	“I don’t work only with Brazilian auteurs,” she adds. “I want auteurs whose stories we are passionate about. We also don’t rely solely on Brazilian funds for financing. We know how to fundraise in Europe, the U.S., and countries like Lebanon. I’ve worked in the U.S. for six years on major films like Noah Baumbach’s ‘White Noise,’ and my DNA comes from learning how to fundraise in a market like the American market and ensure directors whose voices we believe in get to make their films.”

	Faour Auad also notes how important it is to have international directors and productions shoot in Brazil, a movement that has grown in recent years, with films like Michael Almereyda’s “Zero K” shooting in São Paulo. “I think it is very important because we have a wealth of locations, of cast and capable crews,” she says.

	“We also have several new regional incentives and the caliber of our heads of department is one of the greatest in the world,” notes the producer. “We have incredible cinematographers, art directors and costume designers who are all attracting major international directors. I also think it’s interesting that international projects are not only shooting in Brazil to double for another location; they are also interested in telling stories that have Brazil as the background, as it’s the case with ‘Ibicaba.’”

	The production company was present at this year’s Rio Film Festival with the short film “A Casa de Dona Carlota,” directed by Lili Fialho and famed actress Bruna Linzmeyer (“Medusa”) in her directorial debut. Based on Aira Bonfim’s in-depth research, the short film tells the story of Dona Carlota Rezende, the coach of the pioneering female football team Primavera Atlético Clube, in the 1940s. Last year, the banner was at the festival with another high-profile short film, André Hayato Saito’s “Amarela,” which played at the Cannes Film Festival and made the shortlist for Best Live Action Short Film at this year’s Oscars.
	

	MyMama is currently in post-production with João Paulo Miranda Maria’s “I Don’t Even Know Who I Was,” starring Selton Mello and Pia Marais’s “Whyte Lies,” which will see the director return to shoot in Brazil following “Transamazonia.”

title: Why the Boss of Leonine, Germany’s Top Indie Film and TV Company, Is Backing Skydance: ‘David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz Are a Very Strong Team’
description: Fred Kogel, chief executive of Leonine Studios, Germany’s leading independent distribution and production company, is upbeat about the merger of Par
body:
Fred Kogel, chief executive of Leonine Studios, Germany’s leading independent distribution and production company, is upbeat about the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, now part of Skydance. Variety spoke to him about how the merger is likely to affect the film and TV landscape in German-language territories.

	One of the commitments made by Skydance chief David Ellison when he was pushing for the merger was to produce 30-plus movies a year. Kogel is confident that Ellison will deliver.
	

	“What gives me confidence that the number [of movies] will be delivered is that David Ellison comes from a content background and produced great movies with Skydance in the past,” Kogel says. “He is a businessman and a creative guy. He loves the business and he loves making movies.”


	Kogel points to Ellison’s track record as a producer as evidence to support this. “Knowing the production business and knowing the theatrical business, I know what it means to increase the number of theatrical movies,” he says. “It’s a hard feat to achieve. You need long-term development. You need enough projects in the pipeline to build that number up. So, I’m optimistic with him and the management that they will deliver on the number of films.”

	Does Kogel have any concerns about Skydance’s viability, in light of its sizable debt burden?

	“In my opinion, Skydance is a group with extraordinary assets, IPs and possibilities,” he says. “I have complete trust in the people running Skydance. I admire David Ellison because he is an entrepreneur and has proven [his abilities] in the past. I think David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are a very strong team. I also have great respect for Ynon. It requires a vision, a lot of strength and courage, and a great team to achieve what they already have achieved. Of course, it’s a tough market, but it’s a great business to be in. And being the managers they are, I have complete trust that they and their teams can handle this. So, I’m positive. I’m totally positive.”
	

	Kogel sees opportunities for Leonine to produce films for Skydance. “If there is IP that is convincing and that can be produced by us, it could be a natural fit to work with another distributor. That’s what we have already done in the past,” he says.

	Leonine could also produce TV drama series for Skydance. “We are already doing good business with HBO Max as a production unit,” he says. “So, for us, it’s always interesting to be a local producer of premium content and to be aligned with a studio like Skydance, and of course we could help.”

	He adds, “In general, with production, I think it’s a good development. If you come at it from the side of television production, I think it’s also a positive development for us. I mean, we are doing very good business with HBO Max in Germany.

	“HBO Max started [in Germany] at the beginning of the year, and just two weeks ago, we started the first major German original together with HBO Max, ‘Four Blocks Zero’ — the prequel to our very successful TNT series ‘Four Blocks.’ It’s a great production by our banner Wiedemann & Berg Television. It’s a very good collaboration, and additionally we delivered a production by the Beetz Brothers — ‘Clangold,’ the first documentary commissioned by HBO Max in Germany. I see them as a major force in the German commissioning market.

	“Local German productions are very important for all streamers and broadcasters to create a long-term commitment from the German audience. Germany is the biggest TV market in Europe and one of the most important markets in the world. And Skydance as a content powerhouse, with its strong services HBO Max and Paramount+, has the power to invest.”

	The 30-plus movies a year coming from Skydance could be seen as increased competition for Leonine’s distribution business, but Kogel doesn’t see it that way.

	“For me, having been in the distribution business for such a long time, distribution has always been hugely competitive. So, it’s not major news for us,” he says.

	“We are a very competitive local distributor that tries to be at eye level with the international majors, so we are accustomed to a lot of competition. In my opinion, every good movie that enters the German market helps the German market, and the theatrical market in general.
	

	“I don’t see it as a major problem. I think as long as the movies are of high quality — and that’s what I expect — then it’s good for the market. And I mean, we see a big trend, especially in Germany, where the 20-25 best films of the year account for the vast majority of the year’s business. And you simply have to be competitive, and, better still, have one or more of the 25 best films of the year, and that also applies to us. That applies to everybody: Warner, Paramount, Sony, Universal — to everybody. So, it’s a competitive market, and as long as there is really good competition, I’m happy. We have to face that competition. So, I don’t mind getting 10 more films a year in Germany. I would be happy if these are the right films, because we need films that draw the audience to the theatrical market.

	“We are a strong supporter of the theatrical release market, as Leonine, and I’m really very happy if anybody in the business has that commitment.

	“So, our goal is to make the right films that draw people to the cinemas. I think that, with David Ellison and his team’s plans to increase the volume, make quality films, and make audience-pleasing films, we are totally aligned on that.”

	So, is it the quality, not the quantity, of the Skydance films that is important?

	“Yes, it’s the quality. But in the end, I think in most cases the right films will find their way to the market, and that’s the reason why I answer it from the German perspective,” Kogel says. “You must see that, of the approximately 650 films released in Germany each year, at least 200 are German movies, which means 450 are international movies. So, if 10 more international movies were to find their way to the theaters, and if they were the right movies, it would be good for the theaters.

	“For me, it’s a crowded market anyway, and finding the release dates is the most difficult task for our distribution team, as is supporting the films so that they find their way to the audience. We definitely see in the German market that, if we have strong films, other films benefit from that because people will then go to the cinemas. For me, the worst situation is that we have 200 German films and 450 international films and too few must-see movies, which often is the problem, especially with the German productions. So, the discussion for me is not about having 10 more films or 10 fewer films; it’s about having the right films, and if they draw the audience, then that’s a good thing for all of us.”
	

	There may be an opportunity for Leonine to distribute Paramount and Warner Bros. films in German-language countries.

	“That could be a possibility. We buy at least 25 international movies and sometimes carve out an international studio movie and release it in Germany,” Kogel says. “I mean, that’s the kind of business we do, but normally it doesn’t happen if a major studio has a huge distribution operation in Germany — as Warner Bros. has — because then they can release it themselves and don’t need us. But sometimes it happens.”

	There are advantages to having a merged Paramount+/HBO Max streaming group, Kogel says.

	“In the end, I always say it’s good for the whole business if we have strong partners. So, for Leonine, it’s good to have a strong Skydance group in the German market because we can do business with both services. In my opinion in our competitive market the setup will strengthen Paramount+ and that in the end Paramount+ may become a stronger partner under the Skydance banner – at least in the next years. For the moment it’s too early to predict a long-term strategy. But that’s not possible anyway in our business.

	“Competition will increase when it comes to the streamers because a strong HBO Max and a strong Paramount+ are stronger contenders against the other streamers than either would be under separate roofs. For example, if they increase the number of movies to 30-plus, there will be more movies on their platforms. We don’t know yet what will happen in the end. But it will, of course, increase competition, which is generally a good thing for everybody who is in the content business and who wants to produce and license great content. So, for me, it’s a good thing.”

	Leonine has an advantage over other independents in that it is part of a large group, Mediawan, which is headed by Pierre-Antoine Capton, and also includes Plan B.

	“There are, of course, advantages and you have to distinguish between distribution and production. So, in production, we are cooperating in many ways, as we are part of the Mediawan Group, and certain production companies of ours are working closely with production companies within the Mediawan Group. For example: When we produced and released a highly successful German movie called ‘Weekend Rebels,’ it was noticed by Plan B, and together we developed a U.S. version with Plan B, which has now gone directly to Apple. It’s a remake. We work together on co-productions. So, these are very interesting opportunities that Pierre-Antoine Capton and I regularly discuss. What can we do together in non-fiction and fiction, and how can we join forces better?
	

	“When it comes to distribution, I think it’s a different business because distribution is very different from market to market.

	“We are constantly talking about possible future cooperations when it comes to movies: If Mediawan has a successful French movie, we are talking about distributing it in Germany.

	“It’s good that Leonine, as one of Germany’s biggest distributors, is within the Mediawan group. It’s interesting to look at every movie that comes out of the group to see if we can release it or do a carve-out for Germany, Austria and Switzerland.”

	If Warner Bros. and Paramount want to bring more of their production business to Germany, they’ll find that the German production incentive is not as attractive as it could be, Kogel cautions.

	“We are not yet where I want Germany to be in the end, where we could benefit from U.S. studios producing more projects in Germany. Why? It’s easy: We don’t have a tax credit system here that meets the standards of other European countries or of possible future U.S. tax credits, under the new plan.

	“That’s the missing link for Germany to be truly competitive with the other European territories, which already have a tax credit.”

title: Disney+ Taps Amazon Exec Philip Pratt to Oversee Germany, Switzerland and Austria Originals
description:
Amazon MGM Studios exec Philip Pratt has jumped ship to Disney+ where he will oversee original production for Germany, Switzerland and Austria.

	Cu
body:
Amazon MGM Studios exec Philip Pratt has jumped ship to Disney+ where he will oversee original production for Germany, Switzerland and Austria.

	Currently head of original productions at Amazon, he is set to join the Mouse House early next year as a VP, reporting to EMEA content boss Angela Jain.

	“As we grow our local originals for Disney+ in EMEA, we want to back bold, distinctive storytelling that feels relevant to local audiences and can stand out and get noticed,” said Jain. “Philip’s creative track record and experience make him the perfect person to lead that work across Germany, Switzerland and Austria, partnering with exceptional producers and talent to build a slate that gets audiences talking.”
	

	Pratt has been at Amazon MGM Studios for 11 years, where he was responsible for Prime Video’s German original productions including hit YA drama “Maxton Hall,” comedy “LOL: Last One Laughing” and reality competition “The 50.”


	Pratt said: “It is an honour to join The Walt Disney Company. Disney’s ambition for original storytelling is one I’m proud to help build on. I look forward to working with incredibly creative talent to bring stories to Disney+ that entertain, resonate and reach millions of viewers across Germany, Switzerland, Austria and beyond. I envision Disney+ to be a creative home where producers and talent come together, take bold ideas forward and create extraordinary entertainment.”

	Disney+ launched German local originals in 2021, garnering more than 30 noms and 13 wins at German and international awards and entertaining audiences with fare such as “Sam A Saxon”, drama “The Interpreter of Silence” and award-winning series “Call my Agent Berlin.”
	

	Coming up the team have “Vienna Game,” “Nele Neuhaus Monster,” “Westwell” and the recently-announced Swiss production “Under The Ice”.

	Led by new CEO Josh D’Amaro, Disney plans to significantly invest in global Disney+ series, including tripling the volume of international shows. On the horizon are shows such as Poland’s “Breslau 2,” the U.K.’s “Mosquito” and Italy’s “Murder on Lake Garda.”

title: Tsui Hark Pays Emotional Tribute to Nansun Shi, Discusses New Projects and Reflects on AI at Lumière Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
description: LYON, France — Hong Kong filmmaker Tsui Hark paid an emotional tribute to Nansun Shi, his former wife and longtime producing partner, at the Lumière
body:
LYON, France — Hong Kong filmmaker Tsui Hark paid an emotional tribute to Nansun Shi, his former wife and longtime producing partner, at the Lumière Film Festival on Sunday, saying he deeply missed the pioneering producer, who died in July.

	“I miss my partner, Nansun, who helped me on so many projects over so many years,” Tsui said at the start of his masterclass, after watching a montage of highlights from his career.


	Clearly moved and searching for words, he went on: “I would say that my coming here is also a tribute to her. I hope that if she is around us spiritually, she’s happy about what we are doing here.”
	

	Shi, who died on July 13 at the age of 75, was one of the most influential figures in Hong Kong cinema. She co-founded Film Workshop with Tsui in 1984, helping produce and bring to international audiences some of the industry’s defining films. Although the couple divorced, they continued their longstanding professional collaboration and were jointly honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Hong Kong Film Awards in 2025.



	

					Sylvia Chang and Kenny Bee in ‘Shanghai Blues’ (1984)
									Credit: Shaw
	



	A leading figure of the Hong Kong New Wave who helped reinvent the martial arts genre, Tsui is best known for films including “Shanghai Blues,” “Peking Opera Blues,” “Once Upon a Time in China,” “Green Snake” and the “Detective Dee” franchise. The multiple Hong Kong Film Award winner is in Lyon for a retrospective of his work and a masterclass exploring his career.

	Looking ahead, the filmmaker shared details of a new project bringing together Eastern and Western cultures.
	

	“I’m working on a comedy in London,” he said, explaining that the story would bring together people from different cultures to confront a serious problem. “I think we need to put people of different cultures together nowadays to face something serious, so that we have a funny angle looking at this kind of collaboration.”

	Tsui, who said he has always believed in thinking five years ahead rather than simply living in the present, also reflected on the possibilities offered by the growing number of media platforms and how they might be used to create experiences that bring people closer together.

	One idea he is exploring is to create a dreamlike version of a city such as Hong Kong or Beijing, imagined in the future. “The present is so real. Maybe we need something more inspiring to go on.”

	Tsui also reflected on the increasingly blurred boundaries between reality and illusion in a world dominated by advertising, political propaganda, the internet and Artificial Intelligence.

	He described modern society as being constantly influenced by messages designed to shape people’s beliefs and behavior, questioning how much individuals can resist what they are told.

	“We are being very passive to our environment,” he said. “We have a problem with our identity.”

	“I think it’s getting more ridiculous now that we have AI in our culture,” he added. “The funny part of AI is that you’re not sure whether what you see is real or not real.”

	Yet that uncertainty also frightens him. “When you wake up, you don’t know what’s real,” he said, acknowledging that he had no idea what the next five years would bring.

	The filmmaker also spoke about the philosophical dimension of his films, which he sees as a way of questioning the influences shaping people’s perceptions of the world.

	Despite his concerns about contemporary society, Tsui remains convinced that humor has an essential role to play, even when tackling the most serious subjects.

	“The world is so chaotic,” he said. “We have viruses, we have wars, we have economic problems. I don’t know how human beings can survive through all these problems.”

	But cinema, he believes, can help people find a different perspective. “One of the important elements in filmmaking is that maybe we can entertain and inject humor into our belief that the world is still a wonderful place to live.”
	

	Tsui is being celebrated at Lumière with screenings of four of his films: “Shanghai Blues” (1984), “Peking Opera Blues” (1986), “Once Upon a Time in China” (1991) and “Time and Tide” (2000).

	The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through Oct. 18.



	

					Tsui Hark discusses his career at the Lumière Festival.
									Credit: Sarah Mangeret

title: Hollywood Stuntman James Lew's Cause of Death Revealed
description:
Hollywood Stuntman James Lew
                          Cause of Death Revealed
body:
Hollywood Stuntman James Lew
                          Cause of Death Revealed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 12, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            James Lew, the Hollywood stuntman and martial artist, died from congestive heart failure ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            We obtained Lew's death certificate from the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, which shows he died August 23 at an assisted living facility in L.A.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The document lists "end-stage congestive heart failure" as his cause of death. No other significant conditions were listed.
      

            As we first reported ... Lew's wife, Jordanna, told us he died at 73 after battling unspecified health issues.
      
    
            Lew worked as a stunt coordinator and fight stuntman on dozens of movies, including "Star Trek," "Rush Hour," "Lethal Weapon 4," "Action Jackson," and "Timecop."
      
    
            Fans may also remember him from his hilarious fight scene with Charlie Sheen in "Hot Shots! Part Deux."
      
    
            Lew's death certificate says he was cremated.

title: Kelly Osbourne Says She's Gained Nearly 30 Pounds After Grief-Fueled Weight Loss
description:
Kelly Osbourne
                          Ozzy's Death Left Me Unable to Eat ...
body:
Kelly Osbourne
                          Ozzy's Death Left Me Unable to Eat ...
                          Now I'm Re-Gaining Weight
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kelly Osbourne is opening up about her dramatic weight loss following the death of her father, Ozzy Osbourne ... revealing she's since gained nearly 30 pounds after grief left her barely able to eat.
      
    
            The reality star told The Sun she was shocked when she saw photos of herself at the BRIT Awards in February ... admitting she had no idea how thin she'd gotten.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "I couldn't f***ing believe it," Kelly said ... adding she's gained 28 pounds in the six months since.
      

            Kelly insists she wasn't battling an eating disorder ... explaining her grief was so overwhelming that eating made her physically sick.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            At one point, she even visited Ozzy's grave with a candle, begging her late father to help her get better. The next day, her mom, Sharon Osbourne, introduced her to therapist Chris Miller ... whom Kelly credits with saving her life.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Kelly has faced intense scrutiny over her appearance, repeatedly firing back at critics who've commented on her weight.
      
    
            And she's making some big life changes ... moving from Los Angeles to the English countryside with her 3-year-old son, Sidney, following her split from fiancé Sid Wilson.
      
    
            Kelly says she wants her son to have a stable childhood without worrying about school shootings ... and she's even joined his school's PTA.
      
    
            After a devastating stretch, Kelly says she's finally starting to feel like herself again.

title: Indigo Girls Mourn Death of Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
description:
Indigo Girls
                          Mourning Beloved Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
body:
Indigo Girls
                          Mourning Beloved Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Indigo Girls are mourning a heartbreaking loss on the road ... their longtime tour bus driver was killed in a crash in South Carolina, forcing the folk-rock duo to cancel upcoming shows.
      
    
            The driver -- identified by the band as Kirk -- was behind the wheel Friday morning when the bus slammed into a disabled tractor-trailer on Interstate 20 around 6 AM, according to authorities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Kirk was the only person on the bus at the time ... neither Indigo Girls members Amy Ray and Emily Saliers nor any of their crew were onboard.
      

            The cause of the crash remains under investigation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The "Closer to Fine" singers addressed the tragedy in an emotional statement ... saying Kirk had safely driven them thousands of miles over the years and had become a beloved part of their touring family.
      
    
            They wrote, "He was a joyful constant in our lives, and we will miss him dearly."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The duo canceled their Saturday show in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, and postponed Sunday's performance in Wilmington, North Carolina ... with decisions on additional tour dates still to come.
      
    
            Amy and Emily say they plan to return to the road when they're ready ... but for now, they're remembering the man who helped make their shows possible night after night.
